{"baseRefName":"main","body":"Makes two points of TECHNICAL_DESIGN section 5 true that were only convention before: the **kernel** chooses each attempt's ID and each receive locator, and `STAGE_GENERATION` cannot use ones it did not issue. Full description and the list of what is *not* done: `docs/AY4_ATTEMPTS.md`.

**This is an ABI addition, so I'm asking Raj to agree before it merges** (one new command, `BEGIN_ATTEMPT = 13`; the controller and the Netlink conformance tests change with it).

- `BEGIN_ATTEMPT`: kernel picks a random attempt ID (initiator) and a collision-checked, nonzero receive locator; one pending attempt per peer, valid 10 s.
- `STAGE_GENERATION`: only for that attempt, with that locator, once. `EXCHANGE_TX`: only the pending attempt's own INIT/RESPONSE.
- Responder: may only begin the attempt of the last INIT the kernel delivered for that peer (so the controller cannot invent one).
- A completed attempt can still send for 20 s, so the responder can answer duplicate INITs from its cache.
- Controller: asks the kernel through a new `Port::begin_attempt` instead of drawing random values.

**Run on the 6.18 reference VM** (long-lived working copy, not the AN1 master): gateway unit test 1092 assertions (440 new); `ay2_genl` and `ay2_datapath` now go through `BEGIN_ATTEMPT`; `ay2_controller`, `ay4_usage_rekey`, `ay4_silence`, `ay4_soak`, `ay5_runtime`, `demo_reachability` pass in debug and release with a controller built from this branch; `hr4_ip` passes (196 cases) after I updated it to use the issued locators. Sparse, clang, checkpatch unchanged; clippy `-D warnings` clean, 103 controller unit tests.

One honest note: my first full run failed every controller test because the responder consumed the attempt when it installed keys and then could not send its RESPONSE. Review of PR #61 (BEGIN_ATTEMPT = 13), from the controller owner's side. Comment only, not an approval.

What I did and did not do. I read the whole diff at head a9bb964, read control/src/session.rs on that head in full, read the kernel changes in gateway.c, netlink.c and datapath.c, and compared against the diffs of #54 (raj/rj4-live-reload), #52 (adversarial tests) and #51 (BootClock). I checked textual overlap with `git merge-tree` against current main (e0fd460). I did not build anything, did not run cargo, the gateway unit test or any VM suite, and I have not exercised the kernel code. Every statement below about behavior is from reading the code, not from running it. The numbers in the PR description (1092 assertions, 103 controller tests) I have taken on trust.

Summary. I agree with the shape of the ABI: one additive command, an optional ATTEMPT_ID in the request, ID plus LOCAL_RX in the reply, owner-gated, unknown-command behavior unchanged. The controller change in session.rs is small and mostly right. I have no objection to the command. I do have four things I would like addressed or acknowledged (items 1 to 4 below), and the controller unit tests do not yet cover any of the new failure paths (section 3).

1. Controller handling of the failure codes

Port::begin_attempt is wrapped at control/src/session.rs:215-231 and used at :298 (initiator) and :424 (responder).

a) There is no EBUSY. The kernel replaces a pending attempt rather than refusing a second begin (gateway.c:1498 onward, "Replaces any earlier pending attempt"). The only places the controller can call begin twice for one slot are a re-key from Established (which replaces the finished attempt, correct) and a responder handling a second INIT (serialized, correct). I found no controller path that would silently invalidate its own in-flight attempt. That is worth stating in the doc, because the replace behavior is what makes a spoofed INIT matter (item 1, below).

b) ESTALE (116) is retried once with a fresh STATUS, :225-229, same as staging. Fine. Two details. First, the magic number 116 is now in two places (:225 and :387); a named constant would be better. Second, for a responder the kernel checks the given INIT before the incarnation (gateway.c:1514-1520 versus :1530), so after the kernel replaced the peer, a responder begin returns -ENOENT, not -ESTALE, and the retry never runs. This is harmless today because on_exchange (:370) overwrites kernel_incarnation from the event, and the new peer object has no noted INIT anyway, so the INIT is dropped and the initiator's next retransmit works. But the comment at :215-216 ("a kernel that replaced the peer is learned once") is only true for the initiator path. Please say so, or reorder the kernel checks.

c) ENOENT on the responder (no delivered INIT, or INIT older than 10 s, or a different ID than the last INIT) goes to :424-431 and counts as `rejected`. That is the right outcome (drop, wait for the retransmit). Be aware that it inflates `counts.rejected` for events that are not forgeries: two INITs for different attempts queued back to back will make the first one ENOENT by design, because the kernel keeps only the last delivered INIT. Not a defect, but anyone alarming on `rejected` will see it.

d) ETIMEDOUT (110) never comes from begin; it comes from STAGE_GENERATION and EXCHANGE_TX. Controller side:
 - Initiator stage after the 10 s kernel deadline: on_response (:486-499) takes the Err branch, counts a failed attempt and goes Idle for BACKOFF[0]. It does not increment `failures`, so repeated stage timeouts never escalate the backoff beyond 1 s. That asymmetry already existed for other stage errors, but the new deadline makes it reachable on a healthy path: the controller's deadline is checked only in tick() (:248), and on_response does not check it, so a RESPONSE processed between started+10 s and the next tick is staged by the controller but refused by the kernel. The window is small (kernel begin happens after the controller sampled `now`, so the kernel deadline is slightly later than the controller's), but I would add the deadline check to on_response, or at least increment `failures` on this error.
 - In that case the responder has already installed keys and thinks it is Established; the initiator retries after 1 s with a fresh attempt, the responder stages it as the next generation. Recoverable, no wedge.
 - INIT retransmits (:347-361) stop at 7.5 s of the 10 s window (0.5, 1.5, 3.5, 7.5 s, next would be 11.5 s), so they do not hit ETIMEDOUT in normal operation. If tick() is delayed they could; the error is only logged, which is fine.

e) The responder's 20 s post-completion send window against my cache. CACHE_LIFETIME (:51) is 20 s measured from the `now` the event handler was given (:457-460), sampled before stage; the kernel's window (gateway.c:1578-1579) starts at the stage call, so it is never shorter than the controller's cache. Good: the controller never tries to replay after the kernel has closed the window, as long as both clocks tick together. They do not today: the controller uses std::time::Instant (CLOCK_MONOTONIC) and the kernel uses boottime. After a suspend the kernel window can have closed while the controller still thinks the cache is live, and the replay then fails with ETIMEDOUT (logged as "cannot resend RESPONSE", :410-412). #51 (BootClock) removes that skew. The same applies to the 10 s attempt deadline on the initiator. I would land #51 before or together with this, or note the dependency.

f) The 90 s re-key and the 1/2/4/8/16/30 s backoff do not interact with the 10 s and 20 s windows in a way that I could find. Each attempt calls begin itself, so a long backoff simply lets the old attempt expire. One thing to know: a failed begin while Established goes through fail_start (:337-345) and demotes the peer to Idle, so is_established turns false although the kernel still holds working keys. That was already true for a failed exchange_tx; begin adds more ways to hit it (ENODEV when the gateway is stopping, EPERM on a lost lease, repeated ESTALE).

2. An unauthenticated INIT can now clobber the pending attempt (kernel and controller together)

vpt1_peer_note_init is called from rx_exchange (datapath.c, the hunk at line 254) for any well-formed INIT from a peer's configured endpoint, after the rate limiter but before any cryptographic check. The controller then calls begin(given) at session.rs:424 before it runs respond() (:439), because the responder locator has to exist before the RESPONSE can be built. So a forged INIT (source-spoofed to the peer's endpoint, attempt ID of the attacker's choice) causes, in order: note_init overwrites the last-INIT record, begin replaces the peer's pending attempt and resets att_done to false (gateway.c:1566-1569), then respond() fails and the INIT is counted as rejected. Consequences:
 - A genuine INIT delivered just before the forged one is dropped (its ID no longer matches), until the initiator retransmits. Recoverable.
 - More interesting: on an Established responder, the finished attempt's 20 s send window is the thing that lets me answer a duplicate INIT from the cache. A forged INIT replaces that attempt, so the cached RESPONSE for the genuine INIT can no longer be sent (EXCHANGE_TX returns ENOENT because the pending attempt id differs). An initiator whose first RESPONSE was lost would then burn its whole 10 s attempt. Needs an on-path or spoofing attacker, rate-limited by the existing per-peer admit, so low severity, but it weakens the "20 s so the responder can answer duplicates" claim in docs/AY4_ATTEMPTS.md.
 Possible mitigations, in order of how little they change: (i) in the kernel, do not let begin(given) replace an attempt that is att_done and still inside its send window unless the given ID differs and the old keys are already installed (so only a genuinely new INIT may replace it, which is still spoofable, so this is weak); (ii) accept it and document it under "not done"; (iii) in the controller, keep the old cached RESPONSE replayable by sending it through a path that does not require the pending attempt (not possible with the current EXCHANGE_TX rule). I would settle for (ii) plus a test, but I want the author to have looked at it.

Related, not new: the kernel's "last INIT delivered" gate only proves that the kernel saw some INIT from the endpoint, not that it is fresh or authentic. An old INIT replayed after the cache expires (20 s) is accepted by note_init and begin like any other (the 10 s INIT validity is renewed by the replay). That was true before (the controller would re-run respond on it) and the adversarial tests in #52 describe it, so I am not asking for a change here, only noting that "the controller cannot invent an attempt" is not a replay protection.

3. Do the controller unit tests mean anything

The two new decoder tests (vptunnel.rs, a_begin_reply_carries_the_kernels_id_and_locator and a_malformed_begin_reply_is_an_error) are good: they would catch a swapped attribute, a zero locator, a missing attribute and a short ID. There is no test of the request encoder (begin_attempt with given = None must omit ATTEMPT_ID, with Some must include it).

The session tests (session.rs:547-560 TestPort) never exercise the new controller logic, because TestPort::begin_attempt cannot fail and throws away its inputs. By reasoning about mutations:
 - In on_init, pass None instead of Some(&attempt) at :424. TestPort ignores `given` except to echo it back, and on_init discards the returned ID (`Ok((_, locator))`), so every test still passes. This is the one line that makes the responder safe against an invented attempt, and nothing guards it.
 - In start_attempt, ignore the locator begin returned and put a constant in the INIT. both_sides_install_mirrored_keys_and_locators (:755) only checks that the two sides mirror each other and are nonzero, which a constant also satisfies. Survives.
 - Delete the ESTALE retry in Controller::begin_attempt (:225-229). The only stale test (a_stale_kernel_incarnation_is_refreshed_once..., :901) injects the error into stage, not begin. Survives.
 - Replace fail_start at :301 with a bare return (no backoff, so the daemon would retry every tick). No test makes begin fail. Survives, and that mutation is a hot loop against the kernel.
 - The junk-INIT part of forged_and_misdirected_messages_change_nothing (:824-831) now fails earlier, in parse_handshake at :416 rather than in respond(), and still counts rejected+1, so it no longer tests what its name says for the respond() path; it is still a valid test of the new early parse.
 Suggested minimum: make TestPort record each (slot, inc, given) it was called with and accept scripted errors like #52's Kernel does for stage (a VecDeque of errnos). Then add: begin ENOENT on a responder leaves the peer Idle with no RESPONSE and no stage; begin errors on an initiator back off via BACKOFF and do not send an INIT; begin ESTALE refreshes once and retries with the new incarnation; the responder passes the INIT's own attempt ID; the initiator's INIT carries the locator begin returned (assert on the staged local locator).

4. Composition with #54, #52 and #51

#54 (reconfigure). Textually clean: `git merge-tree` of PR #61 with #54 auto-merges session.rs. (#54 and #51 each conflict with current main in daemon.rs and docs/CONTROLLER.md already, independent of this PR; PR #61 does not touch daemon.rs.) Semantically it composes. A kept peer is the same kernel vpt1_peer object (vpt1_gw_commit skips peer_alloc when the slot is policy-only, gateway.c around 1389-1393), so its pending attempt, done attempt, noted INIT and send window all survive, which matches #54 keeping PeerCtl state and the cached RESPONSE. A replaced peer is a new kernel object with att_valid and init_valid false, which matches #54 dropping the cache and starting Idle. So a kept peer holding an attempt is fine, and the cached-response-versus-kernel-window pairing stays consistent in both cases. Two gaps. (1) #54's reconfigure replaces a PeerCtl on a controller-only mismatch (same kernel incarnation but role, key or MTU differs) while the kernel still holds the old pending attempt and send window; the next begin simply replaces them, so this is fine, but no test shows it. (2) #54's tests a_replaced_peer_starts_a_fresh_exchange and friends check c.peers[0].kernel_incarnation, not the incarnation that begin_attempt is called with; once TestPort records its arguments (item 3), add one assertion that the first begin after a reconfigure uses the new incarnation. Also #54's daemon.rs calls Instant::now() at the reload site; when #51 lands that must become clock.now() or the new peer's not_before and the BootClock-derived values will be on different clocks.

#52 (adversarial tests). Textually clean (merge-tree is clean), but it will not compile after this lands: control/tests/adversarial.rs:60 defines `impl Port for Kernel` without begin_attempt, and Port has a new required method. So whichever of #52 and #61 merges second needs a change in #52: add begin_attempt to its fake Kernel. That is also the right place to add the missing coverage. Its tests assert distinct locators and attempt IDs across attempts (the duplicate-cache-expiry and conflicting-second-attempt tests), so the fake must issue a fresh ID and locator per call, and its stage_errors-style script should get a begin_errors twin (EPERM for a lost lease, ENOENT, ESTALE, ENODEV). I would rather #61 is merged first and #52 is rebased, since #52 is test-only, and I will do that rebase.

#51 (BootClock). No textual overlap with #61 (it touches daemon.rs, clock.rs, lib.rs, Cargo.toml, tests/examples.rs, docs). Semantically they belong together: #61 introduces kernel-boottime deadlines (10 s, 20 s) that the controller currently mirrors on CLOCK_MONOTONIC. See 1e.

5. Defects, races and documentation inconsistencies

That drops a genuine INIT, and it closes the 20 s window the responder relies on to answer a duplicate INIT from its cache. It needs a spoofing attacker and is rate-limited, so low severity. I suggest documenting it and pinning it with a test, since I see no cheap kernel-side fix.
